== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:106
- P-174 **A numeral's type exists only at compile time: the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with its four numbers as static parameters; every number type, the library's too, takes a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r` and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`), so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`; the four are naturals of any size, and read as values in a coercion's body they are exact integers, `ZZ`; this implementation's `NN32` bound (P-40) is for sizes. The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", and has libraries define the coercions into integers and rationals (`literals.tex:132-148`); the curator finishes that design, in place of the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). Rows 960 and 981 hold where the tree departs: the digit count of `00.5`, and walk running a numeral type written in a `comprises` clause.

== Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:12-383

\section{Literals}
\seclabel{literals}

\note{We need to check whether the various types and values defined in this section are still correct.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{LiteralExpr} &::=& \texttt{(} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{NumericLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{CharLiteralExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{StringLiteralExpr}\\
\end{Grammar}

Fortress provides boolean literals, \TYP{()} literal, character literals,
string literals, and numeric literals.  Literals are values; they do not
require evaluation.

\note{From here, copied from F1.0$\beta$.}

The literal \VAR{false} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{false}\rrbracket}.
The literal \VAR{true} has type
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
\note{And these are the only values of those types.}

The literal \EXP{()} is the only value with type \TYP{()}.
Whether any given occurrence of \TYP{()} refers to the value \EXP{()} or
to the type \TYP{()} is determined by context.

A character literal has type \TYP{Character}.
Each character literal consists of an abstract character in
\unicode~\cite{Unicode},
enclosed in single quotation marks (for example, `\txt{a}', `\txt{A}',
`\txt{\$}', `\txt{$\alpha$}', `\txt{$\oplus$}').
\marginnote{This is not true: Character literals include ``\b'' and
``LATIN CAPITAL A'', which do not ``consist of'' an abstract character enclosed in
single quotation marks.  I think it's better to remove most of this discussion and
direct the reader to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.
This section should be about {\bf semantics} of literals:
their values and types.}
The single quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' single quotation marks
or a pair of ordinary apostrophe characters (for example, \txt{'a'}, \txt{'A'}, \txt{'\$'}, \txt{'$\alpha$'}, \txt{'$\oplus$'}).
See \secref{preprocessing-character-literals} for a description of how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within character literals,
for example `\txt{APOSTROPHE}' and `\txt{GREEK\_CAPITAL\_LETTER\_GAMMA}'.

A string literal has type \TYP{String}.
Each string literal is a sequence of \unicode\ characters enclosed in double
quotation marks (for example,
``\txt{Hello, world!}'' or ``\txt{$\pi\thinspace r^2$}'').
\marginnote{Again, I think this paragraph should mostly be eliminated and replaced with a pointer to the relevant section of Lexical Structure.

Here's a sentence I wrote as a replacement:
``A string literal (i.e., a sequence of characters enclosed in double quotation marks---see Section 5.10 for details) has type String.''}
The double quotes may be either true typographical ``curly'' double  quotation marks
or a pair of ``neutral'' double-quote characters (for example,
\txt{"Hello, world!"} or \txt{"$\pi\thinspace r^2$"}).
\secref{preprocessing-string-literals} also describes how names of
characters may be used rather than actual characters within string literals.
One may also use the escape sequences \txt{{\char'134}b} and \txt{{\char'134}t}
and \txt{{\char'134}n} and \txt{{\char'134}f} and \txt{{\char'134}r} as described in \cite{JLS}.
Two string literals of the same text denote one object: every evaluation of a
string literal with a given text, wherever it is written, yields the same
string, so that
\EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''} \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''}} is \VAR{true}
(\secref{equivalence}).
A string that a program builds as it runs is another object than a literal of
the same text, unless the operation that builds it answers an existing string;
strings remain reference objects, whose equality of text is their \EXP{=}
(\chapref{objects}).
A concatenation of string literals is itself a string literal
(\secref{static-expr}).
\revision{revival-string-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not
say whether two string literals of the same text are one object.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that they are, on both implementations,
and that a concatenation of two string literals is folded into one literal.}


\note{We may want to eliminate the distinction between simple and compound numerals,
and just distinguish them by whether they have a radix point or not, when necessary
(i.e., ``Numerals may have a radix point.'').  Again,
that distinction is primarily a syntactic one, and can be discussed there if appropriate.}
Numeric literals in Fortress are referred to as \emph{numerals},
corresponding to various expressible numbers.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

Every numeral has a \emph{numeral type} of its own, which exists only when the
program is compiled: no value of a numeral type exists when the program runs.
The static arguments of a numeral type are the numeral's \emph{four numbers}:
the number $n$ of its digits, leading zeros among them;
the number $m$ of its digits after the radix point, which the type of a numeral
without a radix point leaves out, $m$ being $0$;
its radix $r$;
and $v$, the value of its digits, with the radix point deleted, interpreted in
radix $r$.
Each of the four is a natural number, of any size.
A numeral containing only digits has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket},
and a numeral containing a radix point has the type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}.
So \EXP{3.125} has the type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}4,3,10,3125\rrbracket},
\EXP{007} the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}3,10,7\rrbracket}, and
\EXP{3000000000} the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}10,10,3000000000\rrbracket}.
\Library\ declare the two numeral types below the trait \TYP{Numeral}, which
extends \TYP{Number} and has no static parameters: \TYP{NaturalNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyNaturalNumeral} and \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyRadixPointNumeral}, two traits that extend \TYP{Numeral} and exclude
each other.
None of these traits declares a method.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

The radix of a numeral is ten, unless its digits are followed by an underscore
and a radix indicator (\secref{numerals}), which give its radix $r$; such a
numeral has one of the same two numeral types, with its radix as the static
argument $r$.
So \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16}} has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}5,16,912092\rrbracket}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave a numeral
the types \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket} for a numeral without leading zeros,
and \EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}, whose static arguments are
the four numbers.
The revival decided on 9~November 2026 that a numeral's type is the Working
Draft's \TYP{NaturalNumeral} or \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, at the Working Draft's
arities, with the radix as the static argument $r$, and that it exists only
when the program is compiled: the two types with an explicit radix are not
built, since $r$ gives the radix, nor is \TYP{Literal}, and \TYP{Numeral} has no
static parameters.
So the team's draft notes above are answered: no value of a numeral type
exists when a program runs, and this section gives the hierarchy of the
numeral types.}

A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it to a floating-point number before its place is known
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used where a floating-point interval is expected,
it is better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, each of the eight number types (\secref{basic-rationals}) declares
a coercion from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} declare one from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, each generic
over the four numbers, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declares
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)}.
The parameter of such a coercion has no value: its body computes the type's
value from the four numbers, which it reads as values, integers of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\secref{natparams}).
The conversion is exact into the five integer types (\secref{basic-integers})
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and rounds once, to the nearest value of the type, into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.
At a numeral, the compiler instantiates the coercion at the numeral's four
numbers and evaluates it: a value that the Java Virtual Machine holds as an
\texttt{int}, a \texttt{long}, a \texttt{float} or a \texttt{double} is a
constant of the compiled code, and any other value, as one of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}
or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, is made once for the place where the numeral stands, so
that every evaluation of that place yields the same value.

A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares
a coercion from the numeral's type, as each number type of \library\ does and a
type of a program's own may.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral as the number types of \library\
do, through its own coercion from the numeral's type, generic over the four
numbers, whose body computes the type's value from them.
So the Working Draft's floating-point interval can receive
\EXP{3.1415926535897932384} without rounding it first to a floating-point
number:
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Interval}(\VAR{lo}\COLON\mathbb{R}64, \VAR{hi}\COLON\mathbb{R}64)\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} m,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket) =\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{Interval}(\VAR{roundDown}(v, r, m), \VAR{roundUp}(v, r, m))\)\-\-\\\poptabs\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(\VAR{iv}\COLON\TYP{Interval} = 3.1415926535897932384\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{roundDown} and \VAR{roundUp}, functions of the program, round
$v/r^m$ down and up to an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
A numeral at a place whose type is a type of a program's own that declares no
coercion from the numeral's type is a static error: coercion does not chain
(\secref{coercion}), so the numeral is not converted into its default first.
The coercion receives the four numbers of a numeral as written.
A numeral as written under the prefix operator \EXP{-}, as \EXP{-3}, is that
operator of the type applied to the coercion's result for the numeral, so a type
without that operator refuses it; any other static expression of numerals alone
is folded first (\secref{static-expr}) and reaches the type only through the
type's coercion from the folded constant's default type, as \EXP{1/2} through a
coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a type without that coercion refuses it.
A coercion may restrict the four numbers by a \KWD{where} clause that compares
them; a numeral whose four numbers do not meet it is a static error at that
type, as \EXP{300} is at a byte type whose coercion is
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)\;\KWD{where}\;\{v < 256\}}.
At each place where such a numeral stands, the coercion is applied once, with
the type's prefix \EXP{-} where the numeral is negated, not at each evaluation
of the place, so that the numeral there denotes one object, as a string literal
does: two evaluations of one place yield the same object, and each place has its
own application of the coercion.
A numeral type is written in a program only as the type of a parameter, of a
coercion or of an operator, never as the type of a variable, a field or a
functional's result, nor as a static argument, nor as a type that a trait or an
object extends; so the constants \VAR{pi} and \VAR{e} of \library\ are values
of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types, and so gave a
numeral where nothing fixes a type its own type; it said nothing of when a
coercion from a numeral type is applied.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral is converted where it
stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type, and elsewhere into the
default above; that a numeral type is written only as a parameter type; and
that a negated numeral reaches a type of a program's own as the type's prefix
\EXP{-} on the coercion's result.
It decided on 9~November 2026 that every number type, of \library\ and of a
program, receives a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers,
which the compiler instantiates at the numeral and folds, and that a numeral at
a place denotes one value, made once, the same on both implementations.
The interpreter, which has no static types, applies the coercion at the place's
first evaluation and refuses a numeral only there (\secref{revival-numerals}).
The text this replaces, the revival's own of 29~September 2026
(\secref{revival-numeral-type}), named the type of an integer numeral
\TYP{IntLiteral}, the name that the compiled path's own library gave it.}

\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that an
expression of numerals and operators alone is folded exactly into a signed
constant before the static check, on both implementations
(\secref{static-expr}): so \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2},
\EXP{1/2 = 0.5} is \VAR{true}, and the constant is rounded at most once where
a floating-point type is declared, since at a number type of \library\ it is
converted from its exact value; a type of a program's own receives it through
its coercion from the constant's default type.}
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.
Relaxing the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ adds three more values, which
$\mathbb{Q}$ also includes: \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0}, the infinite rationals,
and \EXP{0/0}, the indefinite rational.
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
The advantage of these values is that $\mathbb{Q}$ is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is written as \txt{QQ}.
See \secref{basic-rationals} for its operations.
\revision{revival-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} as three types,
said that a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} assigned to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero} at run time if it is \EXP{1/0}
or \EXP{-1/0}, gave the ASCII names \txt{QQ\_star} and \txt{QQ\_splat}, and
pointed to \secref{advanced-rationals} for the definitions.
The three are one type now, as in \library\ (\secref{basic-rationals}), so no
such assignment converts or throws; that is also the answer to the margin
note's question whether \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} are related by
subtyping or by coercion.}



\subsection{Pi}
\seclabel{pi}

The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
floating-point value or interval value.
In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.

\subsection{Infinity and Zero}

The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.

\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
a floating-point number (discussed in
\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

digitsOf(v: ZZ, r: ZZ, n: ZZ32): String = do
    var s: String := ""
    var k: ZZ := v
    var j: ZZ32 := 0
    while k > big(0) OR j < n do
        d: ZZ32 = (k MOD r).asZZ32
        s := "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"[d] || s
        k := k DIV r
        j += 1
    end
    s
  end

suffix(r: ZZ): String = if r = big(10) then "" else "_" || r.asString end

value object RoundtripNumeral(text: String)
    coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = do
        t = digitsOf(v, r, n.asZZ32)
        w = (n - m).asZZ32
        RoundtripNumeral(t[0#w] || "." || t[w#(m.asZZ32)] || suffix(r))
      end
    coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) =
        RoundtripNumeral(digitsOf(v, r, n.asZZ32) || suffix(r))
    getter asString(): String = text
end

writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, "written back as " || s)
writtenBack(w: RoundtripNumeral, s: String, why: String): () = assert(w.asString, s, why)

content.content:
## B.2 Rats! parsing

There are four grammars, and the build generates four parsers from them with the Rats! generator inside `third_party/xtc/xtc.jar`.

`build.xml` invokes `xtc.parser.Rats` as a forked Java process, once per grammar, through the `buildparser` macro (`build.xml:1400-1424`); the targets are `fortressparser`, `preparser`, `importcollector`, `templateparser` (`build.xml:1427-1450`), all four driven by `parser` (`build.xml:1480-1487`), which `compileAll` depends on.

The generated `.java` files are checked in, and the up-to-date test is mtime-based over the `.rats` sources (`build.xml:1331-1351`), so a fresh checkout looks current — the same trap as the AST nodes.

The macro rewrites the generation date out of the generated header afterwards so regeneration is byte-identical (`build.xml:1416-1423`); that normalization is revival-era.

At run time the four parsers are used as follows.

`ImportCollector` runs first on every component, returning a compilation unit that contains only the imports, so the system can see which grammars a component imports before it can parse it (`compiler/Parser.java:156-176`, called from `macroParse` at `:114`).

`PreFortress` runs on every file whose parse is about to be attempted, purely to produce readable syntax errors: its errors are collected from a log file and reported instead of the packrat parser's (`compiler/Parser.java:415-428`, used at `:323-327`).

`Fortress` is the real parser; after it succeeds, `parser_util/SyntaxChecker` walks the tree for the rules the grammar cannot express (`compiler/Parser.java:346-366`).

`TemplateParser` is never used directly; it is the base that every generated user-grammar parser extends (B.3).

The grammars call into `parser_util/` for everything context-sensitive: juxtaposition and operator precedence are resolved by `precedence_resolver/` from the table in `Operators.java`, which `ant operatorsGen` generates from Unicode data (`build.xml:387-391`).

The compiled type checker does not apply the rule that a numeral type is written
only as a parameter type to the libraries' own files.
A numeral type declares no \EXP{=} with a number type, and a numeral compared by
\EXP{=} with a number goes to the \EXP{=} of the number's type, into whose
parameter type the numeral's own coercion converts it, and not to the top-level
\EXP{=} of \library, whose parameters are of type \TYP{Any} and which the
numeral fits at its default: at a call a numeral goes to the most specific
declaration that takes it (\secref{coercion}).
The interpreter answers \EXP{u = 0} \VAR{true}, and \EXP{u \neq 0}
\VAR{false}, for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and the compiled path does so for a zero of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} or \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}; \TYP{Equality} of \library\ declares
\EXP{\neq} as the negation of the type's own \EXP{=}, and the compiled path's
own library declares \EXP{=} and \EXP{\neq} on each integer type with an
operand of that type (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss},

\nolinkurl{NumeralEqualsNumberCompiled.fss}).
At \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} the compiled path's own library declares no \EXP{\neq},
and its \EXP{=} is the one of its \TYP{Equality}, which calls that library's
\EXP{\sequiv}, whose declaration at \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} calls \EXP{=}: so for

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"
        timeout 600 ../bin/fortress compile "$f" || { echo "LIBRARY BUILD FAILED on $f"; exit 1; }
    done
}

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

main "$@"

"""Turn the raw compile/run outputs of run-ladder.sh into the ladder table.

Reads  explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv  and  raw/<corpus>/<file>.{compile,run}
Writes explorations/compile-ladder/ladder.tsv    (one row per file, diffable)
       explorations/compile-ladder/summary.txt   (the counts and the rankings)

Phase vocabulary, and where each decision comes from:
  parse        a parse-stage refusal (Rats! "Syntax Error", the precedence
               resolver's "Resolution of operator ... failed")
  disambiguate an unresolved or ambiguous name (TypeDisambiguator.java:363,380
               "X is undefined."; "Type name may refer to";
               GraphRepository.java:417 "Could not find an implementation for API")
  typecheck    the Scala checker (TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:95,119
               "Unbound type:"; "Could not check call to"; "Ill-formed type")
  codegen      CodeGen.sayWhat (CodeGen.java:1550-1562 "Can't compile") or any
               CompilerError raised from the codegen packages
  link         `fortress run` fails to load or link the compiled component
  run          `fortress run` throws or exits non-zero
  pass         exit 0, no `fail`/`FAIL` in the output, no exception
               (the interpreter suite's own criterion, FileTests.java:367-371)
"""

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
RAW = os.path.join(ROOT, "raw")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT [--check]      adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does

  rewrite N FILE             FILE holds row N's whole new line (its # cell N
                             or ?, or the seven cells after it); checks it
                             against the template and writes it in the row's
                             place, its earlier line in the history
                             ("rewritten"): the route that corrects a claim,

- gather.5 of climb batch 29's gather (row 960): the Working Draft's `Literal[\v\]`, which climb batch 29's rung T folded into the digit count; since climb batch 29b's rung T the text says that `Literal` is not built, the radix being the static argument `r` (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:146-159`; fork A4); is that the wording meant? Default: T's text, as landed. Review-queue item 473.
- A generic function declared inside a block stops at its declaration, whether it is passed or not: 'Missing type T' (ledger row 1020). Declare it at the top level.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- A numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, not to its default. So `a = 0` is `true` for `a: Any` that holds a zero `NN32`, where the rules' answer is `false` (ledger row 1016). To compare as the rules do, bind the numeral first, as `z = 0`, then write `a = z`.
- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
- A numeral type written in a `comprises` clause loads and runs, as `trait T comprises { NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\] } end` does (ledger row 981). The rules refuse it, as the compiled checker does, and as walk does at load in an `extends` clause or as a static argument: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
program is compiled: no value of a numeral type exists when the program runs.
The static arguments of a numeral type are the numeral's \emph{four numbers}:
the number $n$ of its digits, leading zeros among them;
the number $m$ of its digits after the radix point, which the type of a numeral
without a radix point leaves out, $m$ being $0$;

content.content:
# Source this in every shell that runs Fortress:  source explorations/experiment/env.sh
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=1
# bin/fortress defaults to -Xmx256m (gap ledger row 67); the checks at 4 threads override FORTRESS_THREADS on the command line
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m"
# every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory behind (RatsUtil.getTempDir); 723 of them filled the disk allowance on 2026-09-15.
# Remove only those that no run can still be using: nothing in it written for an hour, and no java process now
# running started before its last write (a run makes its directory after it starts, and reads it until it ends).
(
  oldest=$(ps -C java -o etimes= 2>/dev/null | sort -n | tail -1 | tr -d ' ')
  now=$(date +%s)
  find /tmp -maxdepth 1 -type d -name 'fortress*rats' -mmin +60 -printf '%T@ %p\n' 2>/dev/null |
  while read -r t d ; do
    [ -n "$oldest" ] && [ "${t%.*}" -ge $(( now - oldest )) ] && continue
    [ -n "$(find "$d" -newermt '60 minutes ago' -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ] && continue
    rm -rf "$d"
  done
)

# Rung R (`rung-radix-point-leading-zeros`): record lines for the gather

Climb batch 35, run 1. The fix is `704d6fe747` on `wip/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros`; Appendix I's clause is removed in `535ad0a5c7`. The detail is `REPORT.md` beside this file.

## The finding

A numeral with a radix point now keeps its leading zeros in its digit count on both paths. Claim: `ExprFactory.makeFloatLiteralExpr(Span, String)` keeps the numeral's digits as written, apostrophes and U+202F removed, its leading zeros among them (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1637-1640`), as `makeIntLiteralExpr` does (`:609-632`); `NumeralNumbers.of(FloatLiteralExpr)` counts `n` from that text (`nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java:78`), so `00.5` is `RadixPointNumeral[\3, 1, 10, 5\]` for the checker and for walk. Conditions: every numeral with a radix point that the parser makes; its value, `m` and `v` are unchanged (`x: RR64 = 00.5` prints '0.5' on both paths, old and new). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosWalk.fss` failed on the base through `harness-one.sh`, 'FAIL: a ZZ32: 2 =/= a ZZ32: 3; literals.tex, section "Literals": 00.5 has three digits', and passes ('OK (1 test)'); `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosCompiled.test` failed on the base through `junit.sh`, 'FAIL:  2 =/= 3; ...', and passes ('OK (3 tests)', with its link test). `ant testSystem` (879 tests) and `ant testQuick` (1788, 86 and 263) pass on the fix's code; the count stage and the distance stage are the same as the last landed gate's, total 0 each. What it means: a program's own coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` reads the digit count that P-174 and `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:101` give. A checker message that quotes such a numeral shows it as written ('The numeral 00.5 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Small.'), and a folded `MIN`, `MAX` or `|x|` that answers a written radix-point operand keeps its text, so its numeral type in a checker message counts the operand's zeros (`RadixPointNumeral[\3,1,10,5\]` for `00.5 MAX 0.1`); no program and no library coercion reads a folded constant's numbers (P-174; the curator's question in `REPORT.md`).

## FACTS.md

Under "Landed semantics", a new entry:

- **A numeral with a radix point keeps its digits as written in the node that both paths read, so its digit count `n` counts its leading zeros: `00.5` is `RadixPointNumeral[\3, 1, 10, 5\]`.** `ExprFactory.makeFloatLiteralExpr` removes only apostrophes and U+202F from the numeral's text (`nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1637-1638`), as `makeIntLiteralExpr` does, and `NumeralNumbers.of` counts `n` from that text for the checker and for walk (`nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java:71-100`); the value, `m` and `v` are read as before. So `00.5` was `RadixPointNumeral[\2, 1, 10, 5\]`, where P-174 and `literals.tex:101` make `n` 3. The edit deletes the four lines of the trim (fork R1): the node keeps the digits as written, apostrophes and narrow no-break spaces removed, its leading zeros among them, as an integer numeral's node already does. The values are unchanged: `intPart` is read by `new BigInteger(digits, base)`, which takes leading zeros, and `m` and `v` come from the digits after the point. Now at `ExprFactory.java:1637-1640`:

```java
        // Delete every apostrophe and U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE
        s = s.replace("'", "").replace(" ", "");

        int dotLoc = s.indexOf('.');
```

## The finding

A numeral with a radix point now keeps its leading zeros in its digit count on both paths. Claim: `ExprFactory.makeFloatLiteralExpr(Span, String)` keeps the numeral's digits as written, apostrophes and U+202F removed, its leading zeros among them (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1637-1640`), as `makeIntLiteralExpr` does (`:609-632`); `NumeralNumbers.of(FloatLiteralExpr)` counts `n` from that text (`nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java:78`), so `00.5` is `RadixPointNumeral[\3, 1, 10, 5\]` for the checker and for walk. A checker message that quotes such a numeral shows it as written ('The numeral 00.5 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Small.'), and a folded `MIN`, `MAX` or `|x|` that answers a written radix-point operand keeps its text, so its numeral type in a checker message counts the operand's zeros (`RadixPointNumeral[\3,1,10,5\]` for `00.5 MAX 0.1`); no program and no library coercion reads a folded constant's numbers (P-174; the curator's question in `REPORT.md`).

A checker message that quotes such a numeral shows it as written ('The numeral 00.5 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Small.'), and a folded `MIN`, `MAX` or `|x|` that answers a written radix-point operand keeps its text, so its numeral type in a checker message counts the operand's zeros (`RadixPointNumeral[\3,1,10,5\]` for `00.5 MAX 0.1`); no program and no library coercion reads a folded constant's numbers (P-174; the curator's question in `REPORT.md`).

## FACTS.md
